query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: The emergence of brittle behavior in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy is governed by the formation of nanoscale chemical fluctuations and the resulting grain boundary decohesion, which can be triggered by high strain rate shear and dynamic amorphization.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure
generation.intervention: High strain rate shear (e.g., 10^(-2) s^(-1)) at elevated temperatures (e.g., 1173 K)
generation.conditions: Ultra-high vacuum environment to mitigate oxidation and mixed metal-oxide film formation
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary decohesion and nanoscale chemical fluctuations
generation.mechanism: Dynamic amorphization and inverse Hall-Petch behavior leading to grain boundary decohesion
generation.predicted_outcome: A decrease in toughness by 20% relative to the initial baseline, with a corresponding increase in brittleness
generation.baseline: Initial single-phase high-entropy alloy with a toughness of 100 MPa·m^(1/2)
generation.boundary: Strain rate of 10^(-2) s^(-1) and temperature of 1173 K
generation.uncertainty: The exact relationship between grain boundary decohesion and nanoscale chemical fluctuations is not fully understood, and the role of other factors such as impurities and defects is not well established

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of the high-entropy alloy under high strain rate shear and dynamic amorphization conditions, with and without the presence of nanoscale chemical fluctuations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the toughness of the high-entropy alloy does not decrease by at least 15% relative to the initial baseline under the specified conditions, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSuperplastic metals that exhibit exceptional ductility (>300%) are appealing for use in high‐quality engineering components with complex shapes. However, the wide application of most superplastic alloys has been constrained due to their poor strength, the relatively long superplastic deformation period, and the complex and high‐cost grain refinement processes. Here these issues are addressed by the coarse‐grained superplasticity of high‐strength lightweight medium entropy alloy (Ti43.3V28Zr14Nb14Mo0.7, at.%) with a microstructure of ultrafine particles embedded in the body‐centered‐cubic matrix. The results demonstrate that the alloy reached a high coarse‐grained superplasticity greater than ≈440% at a high strain rate of 10−2 s−1 at 1173 K and with a gigapascal residual strength. A consecutively triggered deformation mechanism that sequences of dislocation slip, dynamic recrystallization, and grain boundary sliding in such alloy differs from conventional grain‐boundary sliding in fine‐grained materials. Measurements of grain boundary energy are sensitive to thermally-driven grain boundary segregation (and possibly phase separation) of impurities. This value is relatively high for metals,, and may imply a propensity for localized cohesive failure or fracture at the boundaries. Grain boundary decohesion has been recently shown to occur readily for this alloy due to segregation and nanoclustering of Cr, Ni and Mn at elevated temperature, and these failures typically originate along HAGBs and at triple junctions. In the present work there is no significant evidence of grain boundary segregation, and this is reasonable as a negligible increase in temperature is expected for these sliding conditions. This suggests that this alloy may also be prone to grain boundary decohesion without significant segregation and phase separation, i.e., when it is a solid solution. AbstractEnergy efficiency is motivating the search for new high-temperature (high-T) metals. Some new body-centered-cubic (BCC) random multicomponent “high-entropy alloys (HEAs)” based on refractory elements (Cr-Mo-Nb-Ta-V-W-Hf-Ti-Zr) possess exceptional strengths at high temperatures but the physical origins of this outstanding behavior are not known. Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations. This finding is surprising because plastic flows in BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys are generally controlled by screw dislocations. We use the insight and theory to perform a computationally-guided search over 107 BCC HEAs and identify over 106 possible ultra-strong high-T alloy compositions for future exploration.Subject terms: Mechanical engineering, Mechanical properties, Computational methods The strength in BCC high-entropy alloys is associated with the type of mobile dislocations.
